name: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state

matching.reasoningTemplate: Marked hyperglycaemia with hyperosmolar altered sensorium and minimal ketosis suggests HHS rather than DKA.

redFlags: Profound dehydration — careful fluid/insulin; precipitant often infection

clinicalPearls: Typical patient is an older adult with type 2 diabetes presenting after a several-week prodrome of polyuria, weight loss and falling oral intake, progressing to confusion, lethargy or coma (p.3219).
Examination reflects profound dehydration and hyperosmolality: hypotension, tachycardia and altered mental status (p.3219).
Features classically ABSENT in HHS that are seen in DKA: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and Kussmaul respirations (p.3219).
HHS and DKA lie on a continuum of hyperglycaemia; up to one-third of patients have overlapping features of both (p.3216).
Plasma glucose in HHS is usually markedly higher than in DKA and may exceed 55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219).
A debilitating condition (e.g. prior stroke, dementia) or a social situation that limits access to water frequently contributes to HHS by impairing water intake (p.3218-3219).
Worldwide reported cases of both HHS and DKA are rising for reasons that are not clear (p.3216).
harrison.pathophysiology: HHS arises from RELATIVE insulin deficiency combined with inadequate fluid intake. Insulin deficiency drives hepatic glucose overproduction (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis) and impairs glucose uptake by skeletal muscle. The resulting hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with intravascular volume depletion that is worsened by inadequate fluid replacement. The reason ketosis is absent is not fully understood; the insulin deficiency is presumed to be only relative and less severe than in DKA, and some studies show lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels in HHS than in DKA, with possibly reduced hepatic ketone synthesis or an insulin/glucagon ratio that does not favour ketogenesis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both HHS and DKA (p.3217-3219).
additionalDifferentials: Diabetic ketoacidosis (and the DKA/HHS overlap presentation) (p.3216).
Other causes of an altered/hyperosmolar sensorium - the differential for hyperosmolar coma includes uremia, nonketotic hyperosmolar states and other metabolic derangements (p.3216, general).
additionalInvestigations: Plasma glucose - typically markedly elevated, may be >55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219).
Corrected serum sodium - measured Na may be normal or low, but corrected Na (add ~1.6 meq/L for each 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] rise in glucose) is usually elevated (p.3219).
Renal function (BUN/creatinine) - prerenal azotaemia from volume depletion; creatinine typically moderately raised (p.3219).
Ketones/beta-hydroxybutyrate - absent or only mild; serum beta-hydroxybutyrate <1.0 mmol/L; any moderate ketonuria is usually due to starvation (p.3219).
Acid-base status - acidosis absent or mild; a small anion-gap metabolic acidosis may reflect raised lactic acid (p.3219).
redFlags: HHS carries a substantially higher mortality than DKA (up to ~15% in some series), reflecting older patients, more pronounced dehydration and serious precipitating events with comorbidities (p.3219).
Hyperosmolar state must be reversed gradually - too-rapid correction risks worsening neurologic function (p.3219).
Precipitant is often a serious concurrent illness - myocardial infarction, stroke, sepsis, pneumonia or other severe infection - which must be actively sought (p.3219).
harrison.prognosis: Even with appropriate treatment, HHS has a substantially higher mortality rate than DKA, reported up to about 15% in some clinical series. The worse outlook reflects that HHS patients are usually older, have more profound fluid losses and dehydration (developed over days to weeks), are more likely to have mental status changes, and more often have a life-threatening precipitating event with accompanying comorbidities (p.3219).
pitfalls: A normal or low measured serum sodium can be falsely reassuring - it must be corrected for hyperglycaemia, after which it is usually elevated and reveals a profound water deficit (p.3219).
Mild ketonuria may be present but is typically from starvation, not from ketoacidosis - it should not redirect the diagnosis away from HHS (p.3219).
Fever may be absent even when infection is the precipitant; signs of infection should be sought regardless (p.3217, DKA section, applicable to acute hyperglycaemic crises).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a graded severity classification specific to HHS (unlike DKA, which is graded mild/moderate/severe by pH, bicarbonate and mental status). HHS is instead defined by marked hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm/L) and the relative absence of ketosis/acidosis, on a continuum with DKA (p.3218-3219).
